newsitem.title: UK: Film minister hails new dawn for UK movies.
newsitem.headline: Film minister hails new dawn for UK movies.

text.p: Britain's film minister Tom Clarke on Monday hailed a new dawn for the national film industry, saying that native talent, tax breaks and the commitment of the new Labour government should transform a cottage industry into a consistent force in world cinema.

Speaking to actors, producers and distributors at the Edinburgh Film Festival, Clarke said the stage was set for an industry that has produced one-off hits like "Four Weddings and a Funeral" to realise its full potential.
"The British film industry has for many years produced brilliant individual efforts but has rarely succeeded in delivering consistently good results," said Clarke.
"We have the talent to do it and now we have the tax regime, the financial resources and a government ready and determined to give that backing," he said.

The Labour government that swept to power in May has announced a string of initiatives aimed both at encouraging film production in this country and improving distribution to ensure that British films reach cinema screens now dominated by Hollywood blockbusters.

Film companies will be allowed to write off the entire cost of movies with budgets of up to 15 million pounds ($23.8 million), three film consortiums have been given 90 million pounds over the next six years and Clarke has set up a film policy review group aimed at doubling the box office share of British films.

More than 100 films were produced in Britain last year but almost half failed to get national cinema releases. Yet cinema admissions in Britain have jumped from 55 million people in 1984 to 123 million in 1996, spurred by investment in vast new multiplexes.

Cult films like "Trainspotting" have won plaudits abroad but the 1997 Oscar-winning hit "The English Patient" -- directed by Briton Anthony Minghella and with a largely British cast -- had to look to the United States for finance.

Despite patchy funding, the number of films made in Britain is 30 percent up on three years ago and the Edinburgh Film Festival is showcasing more than 20 new British movies including "Secrets and Lies" director Mike Leigh's haunting examination of the last 15 years "Career Girls".

The Edinburgh Film festival, which started in 1947, has become the most comprehensive commercial market for British films in the world through a forum bringing distributors, producers and film students together.
Last year more than 250 delegates from all over the world attended the special NBX forum, including festival programmers and acquisition executives from Hollywood.

Clarke, who enjoyed a brief cinematic career of his own in the 1970s when he entered a short film at the Cannes film festival, is the first British government minister for years whose brief is directed specifically at developing the film industry. Under the previous Conservative administration the job was seen as a part-time junior post.
David Puttnam, producer of the British 1970s hit "Chariots of Fire", is delighted that years of vigorous campaigning appear to have paid off.

"At last we seem to have a government which is not embarrassed to recognise the huge economic and cultural benefits of a thriving, dynamic film industry," he wrote in a Guardian newspaper article last month. ($ = 0.630 British Pounds)
